decision: Datum is the main focus; the job search runs on an honest profile, saying yes to recruiters who reach out
why: Phone screens keep stalling on experience mismatch, and a launched product with real users is your strongest resume line. Fix LinkedIn and resume first so inbound matches your real level.
revisit: End of November, or if money gets tight sooner

decision: Monarch-style app is the next build project, after Datum
why: You want repeated design-and-build reps. Monarch's moat and bank-data costs still argue against it as a business, so treat it as a build project first and judge the business case later.
revisit: When Datum is stable in production and moves to marketing and growth

decision: Datum version one: Florida and commercial clients only
why: Florida's core business records are free bulk downloads, and checking businesses rather than people keeps Datum away from consumer-report rules under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
revisit: After 10 paying users: expand to more states

decision: Mobile-friendly web app first; native iPhone and Android apps later
why: One codebase, no app-store review or in-app payment rules, and contractors still use it from their phones.
revisit: When users need push notifications or offline use

decision: Workflow first; an agent only for long-tail lookups, behind human review
why: Most steps are predictable, so plain code is cheaper, faster, and testable. Telling a contractor the wrong company has liens is a legal problem, not a bug.
revisit: Full design and architecture session, then if long-tail lookups become most of the work

decision: Daily Snowflake and dbt practice moves to Datum's real-data pipeline; credit-stream gets Airflow, then maintenance
why: Public records that change daily teach incremental loads, change history, and entity resolution. More synthetic data in credit-stream wouldn't.
revisit: Starts now; check after credit-stream's Airflow work ships

decision: Find contractors in parallel with the build, leading with a free report instead of asking for an interview
why: Cold asks got no response. A free check on a client they're actually worried about gives them a reason to reply, and a $50 gift card for 15 minutes covers the rest. Flyers at supply houses, persistent email follow-up, and small local ads add reach.
revisit: After the first 20 outreach attempts: compare which channel got replies. Gift card raised from $25 to $50 on Oct 12.

decision: Where Datum's data lives: Snowflake for the pipeline, Postgres for the app
why: Real pipeline practice is worth the spend. Guardrail: a small warehouse that suspends after 60 seconds, plus a Snowflake resource monitor that caps monthly credits, so a mistake can't run up a surprise bill.
revisit: Full design and architecture session

decision: One Snowflake stage per Sunbiz file type. Company filings use sunbiz_stage now; fictitious names and federal tax liens each get their own stage when added.
why: Each load reads its whole stage, so there are no folder paths to remember and no filename filters to maintain. It's the simplest setup that can't mix file types.
revisit: If we load more than about five Sunbiz file types, or once loads are automated

decision: Raw keeps each state record line untouched; staging parses it, and damaged lines are flagged (is_well_formed), not dropped
why: If a field position is wrong, the fix is one staging file with no reload, and data problems stay visible instead of silently disappearing.
revisit: If flagged rows exceed about 1% of a load

decision: Development environment only for now (DEV_STAGING, DEV_MARTS); no production environment yet
why: Nothing reads the data yet, so a production environment would add complexity with no user.
revisit: When the web app starts reading the data

decision: Add REST API ingestion in Python: credit-stream gets FRED API to S3 with boto3 to Snowflake; Datum gets a real API source (CourtListener) in version 1.1
why: Interview feedback: interviewers want to see an API endpoint rather than a flat file, Python written as functions or classes, boto3 for AWS, and validation before data lands. Both projects so far ingest bulk files only.
revisit: After the credit-stream API ingestion ships and the repo is shared

decision: Week 3 income is the BasePoint repo share: the FRED API function, validation and a test come before the evaluation set and flyer if time is short
why: The repo-sharing promise has a deadline; the answer key and flyer don't. The Income, Build and Grow cards have carried since Oct 22–24 with no reported progress.
revisit: Next Sunday's re-plan

decision: Ship search v1 (LLM extraction, then Jaro-Winkler name search); reject both retrieve-then-rerank variants
why: The rerank variants traded cheap errors (the right company lower on the shortlist) for expensive ones (a confident wrong company). A wrong identity in a risk report costs far more than an extra shortlist row.
revisit: When the 50-case test set from real inputs is ready

decision: Week 4 order: BasePoint repo share first, then the 50-case evaluation set, with the first supply-house visit early in the week
why: No progress has been reported since Oct 29, and Income, Build and Grow cards have carried since Oct 30. The repo share has an external deadline; the flyer visit is cheap and the only route to contractor conversations.
revisit: Replaced by the Nov 2 MVP re-plan (launch-ready Nov 13)

decision: MVP scope: a private, mobile-friendly web app with Sunbiz, IRS federal tax liens, DBPR licenses and discipline, Duval liens, and risk flags with a citation on every line. Launch-ready Fri Nov 13; interviews start Nov 10
why: A Sunbiz-only report isn't worth a contractor's time; collating several public sources is the product.
revisit: Sat Nov 7 re-plan (Nov 13 at risk), then the Nov 13 close-out

decision: Risk flags from public records in version one, not a numeric score or bureau data
why: Business scores like FICO SBSS blend the owner's personal credit (Fair Credit Reporting Act territory), bureau reports cost $40–200+ each, a score needs outcome data we don't have, and it breaks the no-black-box commitment.
revisit: After 20 interviews, or once outcome data exists

decision: Duval liens: a human-collected pilot plus a Chapter 119 request for the full index; no automated retriever until counsel reviews the click-through gate
why: Recon found no bulk file and no API, and automating the disclaimer gate is legally unresolved.
revisit: Replaced by d21 on Nov 5

decision: Serving layer: Postgres with pg_trgm (trigram fuzzy search) on Railway answers lookups; Snowflake only runs the builds
why: Waking a suspended X-Small warehouse costs about $0.033 per lookup vs about $0.00035 for the Haiku call, and adds seconds. Postgres also keeps the app alive after the Snowflake trial ends around Nov 15.
revisit: At 100 lookups a day, or if the database outgrows the Railway plan

decision: Linking rule: flags attach only on CONFIRMED links (same name once legal suffixes are removed and the same ZIP code, or the only company with that name). AMBIGUOUS shows as "possible match: verify"
why: Accusing the wrong company of a lien is the most expensive error Datum can make (asymmetric error costs).
revisit: If CONFIRMED coverage is under 50% of lien records

decision: Web stack: FastAPI + server-rendered Jinja templates + Pico CSS, no JavaScript framework
why: Simplest correct option, mobile-first, and all Python, the language you're building skills in.
revisit: When the watchlist needs live interactivity

decision: Duval liens come from the Clerk's free bulk recording index over secure FTP (replaces d17). Individuals' records stay in raw; staging keeps only parties that match a company
why: The Clerk offered the full index at no cost on Nov 4: the official channel, complete, and no click-through gate. Dropping individuals at staging keeps Datum businesses-only.
revisit: If their terms restrict commercial use, or access isn't live by Nov 9 (then hand-collect for the demo)

decision: Week 5 re-plan: the first supply-house donut run is fixed for Monday Nov 9 and gets done before any new Build work; the 50-case set and BasePoint repo share stay in front of the matcher target
why: The donut run has slipped from Oct 15 to Oct 30 to Nov 8, and the scorecard still shows 0 contractor conversations. Customer conversations are the largest open risk for Datum.
revisit: Nov 15, after the first week of conversations

decision: Email outreach runs as an agent on two weekday scheduled tasks: a 1:17 AM night run (research, subagent verification, drafts) and a 7:12 AM morning run (log sends, sort replies, follow-up drafts). It starts in approve mode: Andres sends every email himself
why: Outreach was the bottleneck and he wants about 95% of it automated, but one bad unattended batch sent in his name can damage the domain for months. Approve mode keeps a human check while the drafts prove themselves.
revisit: Switch config send_mode to auto when 30+ initial emails are sent, 10% or fewer were edited, and bounces stay under 2% (the morning push says when)

decision: Email outreach targets Florida contractors only, using emails the business publishes itself, verified against Sunbiz and DBPR by an independent subagent
why: The free report covers Florida companies in version one. Guessed addresses bounce and scraping runs into terms-of-use limits.
revisit: When a second state goes live

decision: Send from andres@datumriskservices.com on Google Workspace (SPF, DKIM, DMARC all pass); no second sending domain; home address in the footer for now
why: Cloudflare forwarding plus Gmail send-as fails DMARC and lands in spam. At 15 emails a day a second domain solves a problem we don't have. CAN-SPAM requires a postal address; home is legal today.
revisit: Second domain if the daily cap goes past 30 or bounces climb; swap the home address for a USPS PO box when one is rented

decision: Sunbiz is a soft check for outreach: an active DBPR license plus the company's own website and published email is enough to send an email
why: search.sunbiz.org blocks automated access, so the first run held 10 good prospects. The email makes no claim about the company; Sunbiz verification matters for reports, which already use the bulk files.
revisit: If a sent email reaches a dissolved or wrong company, or when the agent can check Sunbiz against Datum's own bulk-file data

decision: The Gmail drafts box holds at most 30 outreach drafts at a time, set by draft_box_cap in the ledger's config tab. The night run drafts only enough new emails to refill the box, and once send_mode is switched to auto, the morning run sends the drafts the night run already reviewed, up to daily_cap each weekday.
why: On Nov 19 the box held 69 drafts, because the night run added 15 every weeknight while about 10 a day were sent by hand. Drafts that wait for days go stale, and a full night run costs about 20 minutes of Opus. With a cap, the two runs become a steady loop in which about as many emails are researched each night as are sent each morning.
revisit: Raise or lower draft_box_cap or daily_cap in the config tab if replies call for more or fewer emails. The switch to auto-send still waits on the d23 targets, which are 30 or more initial emails sent, 10% or fewer edited before sending, and a bounce rate under 2%.
